description:
Found while starting fz-5xp.12, and it is a prerequisite for that ticket's
first work item.

    built = "a" <> "b"
    m = %{"ab" => 1, built => 2}

    elixir  %{"ab" => 2}   count 1   m["ab"] -> 2     (the later key wins)
    interp  %{"ab" => 2}   count 1   m["ab"] -> 2     agrees
    run     %{"ab" => 1}   count 1   m["ab"] -> 1     SILENTLY WRONG

A duplicate binary key in a map literal keeps the FIRST value on the JIT door
instead of the last. No error.

ROOT CAUSE, in runtime/src/heap/key_cmp.rs: the map is a flat SORTED array, but
its two relations disagree about binary keys.

  * `same_value_ref` compares bitstrings STRUCTURALLY (`bitstring_like_eq`).
  * `map_key_cmp_refs` orders them by `value_ref_sort_payload`, which for a
    heap value is its ADDRESS.

So two structurally-equal binaries at different addresses are EQUAL to lookup
and UNEQUAL to the sort. They do not become adjacent, so a dedup driven by the
ordering never sees them as the same key. `map_key_cmp_refs` also splits
BITSTRING from PROCBIN on the tag, so the same content stored inline versus
shared sorts into different groups while comparing equal.

Lookup survives only because it is a LINEAR SCAN using the structural relation
-- `m[built]` does find the entry today. That is why the bug hid: the slow path
is the correct one.

WHY IT BLOCKS fz-5xp.12. That ticket's first item is "binary search in
Heap::read_map_addr_value_ref (the array is already sorted)". The array IS
sorted -- by a relation that does not agree with the equality the search must
use, so a binary search over it would MISS a key the scan finds. The ordering
has to agree with the equality before the array is searchable at all.

WHY IT IS P1. `Json.decode` builds maps whose keys are binaries constructed at
runtime, and duplicate keys are legal in JSON input with last-one-wins the
common rule. This is the goal program's central data structure.

DONE = a map's key order agrees with its key equality: bitstrings ordered by
CONTENT, with BITSTRING and PROCBIN of equal content ordered together. Then
equal keys collide, the later value wins on every door, and the array becomes
binary-searchable. Expect map ITERATION ORDER to change, which is observable
via `Enum`/`dbg` -- check it against Elixir, whose small maps are term-ordered,
rather than against the current goldens.
title: [BUG] A map's key ORDER disagrees with its key EQUALITY, so equal binary keys do not collide
